-## 1. One-time setup
+## Part 0. ATLAS in one minute
 
-ATLAS runs on **macOS or Linux** (D13). Each person installs their own copy and uses their own accounts and models (ADR-007). Windows isn't supported yet; WSL2 may come later.
+ATLAS is a program you run on your own computer. You give it a software task for one of your GitHub repositories, for example "Add Google OAuth login". ATLAS then:
 
-### 1.1 Prerequisites
-| Tool | Why | Check |
-|---|---|---|
-| `git`, `gh` | Repository and GitHub operations | `gh --version` |
-| Python 3.12, `uv`, Node 24 | ATLAS itself | `python3.12 --version` |
-| Colima + Docker CLI | Test sandbox (D11). On Linux, also QEMU + KVM | `colima version` |
-| A secret store | macOS Keychain (built in) or, on Linux, a Secret Service provider such as GNOME Keyring or KWallet | — |
-| **At least two agents from different model families** | They fill the roles. Reviews must come from a different family than the author (ADR-005). See §1.6 | per agent |
+1. asks one AI agent to **plan** the work as small phases;
+2. asks a **different** AI agent to **challenge** the plan;
+3. waits for **you** to approve the plan;
+4. for each phase: an agent **writes the code**, ATLAS **runs the tests** in a locked-down container, another agent **reviews** the code, and a QA step **checks** it;
+5. opens a pull request and waits for **you** to approve the merge.
 
-ATLAS never signs in to agent tools for you, and never reads the logins those CLIs manage. ATLAS reads only two kinds of credential, both from your OS secret store:
-- the per-project GitHub PAT (§1.3), passed only to its own `git`/`gh` processes;
-- an API key, but only for an agent you set to `billing: api_key` (§1.5), passed only to that agent's process.
+You stay in control: nothing is built before you approve the plan, and nothing is merged before you approve the merge.
 
-If an agent logs out, ATLAS pauses it and tells you which command to run.
+### Words used in this guide
+| Word | Meaning |
+|---|---|
+| **Agent** | An AI coding tool ATLAS can use, such as Claude Code, Codex, or a local model. You bring your own |
+| **Role** | A job in the workflow: *architect* (plans), *challenger* (attacks the plan), *developer* (writes code), *reviewer* (reviews code), *qa* (checks the result) |
+| **Model family** | Who made the model, e.g. Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT/Codex), Google (Gemini), Alibaba (Qwen), Meta (Llama). Reviews must come from a different family than the author |
+| **Phase** | One small, separately mergeable piece of a task |
+| **Candidate commit** | The exact commit that was tested and reviewed. Only this commit may be merged |
+| **Sandbox** | The Docker container, in its own virtual machine, where ATLAS runs tests. Tests never run directly on your computer |
+| **PAT** | A GitHub *Personal Access Token*: a password-like key that lets ATLAS work on one repository |
+| **Dashboard** | ATLAS's web page. It runs only on your computer, at `127.0.0.1` |
+| **BLOCKED / PAUSED** | ATLAS stopped and needs something from you. [Part 7](#part-7-troubleshooting-what-each-state-means) explains each one |
+
+LangGraph is ATLAS's **internal** workflow engine (ADR-001, ADR-006). You never use it directly; there's nothing to install, configure or pay for.

-```

-- Data lives in `~/.atlas/` (databases, logs, artefacts). Phase 10 adds an optional login service: `launchd` on macOS, a `systemd --user` unit on Linux.

+## Part 1. Prepare your computer
+
+### Step 1. Check your operating system
+**Available:** [today]
+ATLAS runs on **macOS** or **Linux** (D13). Windows isn't supported yet; WSL2 may come later.
+
+Each person installs their own copy of ATLAS and uses their own accounts and models (ADR-007). There is no shared, hosted ATLAS.
 
-### 1.3 GitHub token per project (D3) **[P1 checks, P5 use]**
-Store your PAT in the OS secret store under ATLAS's name for the project. Both commands prompt for the token without echoing it:
+### Step 2. Install the required tools
+**Available:** [today]
+| Tool | Why ATLAS needs it | Check it's installed |
+|---|---|---|
+| `git` | Works with your repositories | `git --version` |
+| `gh` (GitHub CLI) | Opens pull requests and reads CI results | `gh --version` |
+| Python 3.12 | ATLAS is written in Python | `python3.12 --version` |
+| `uv` | Installs ATLAS's Python packages | `uv --version` |
+| Node 24 | Builds the dashboard | `node --version` (should print `v24…`; on macOS, follow Homebrew's printed note to add `node@24` to your `PATH`) |
+| Colima + Docker CLI | Runs the test sandbox (D11) | `colima version` and `docker --version` |
+| Linux only: QEMU + KVM | Lets Colima run its virtual machine on Linux | `ls /dev/kvm` |

-### 1.4 Test sandbox (D11) **[P4]**

-If the sandbox isn't ready, projects show `BLOCKED(no_test_sandbox)` with the reason. Nothing runs unsandboxed.
+### Step 3. Set up at least two agents from different model families
+**Available:** [today]
+ATLAS needs **at least two agents from different model families**, because a change must be reviewed by a model from a different family than the one that wrote it (ADR-005). Choose one of these setups:
+
+| Setup | Agents you need | Notes |
+|---|---|---|
+| **A. Recommended** | Claude Code + Codex + Antigravity | Uses your existing subscriptions |
+| **B. Fully local** | Two or more open-weight models from different families, e.g. Qwen and Llama, served by Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM or `llama-server` | No subscriptions; code stays on your machine |

+**For setup A:**
+1. **Install** each tool by following its official install guide:
+   - Claude Code: <https://www.anthropic.com/claude-code>
+   - Codex CLI: <https://github.com/openai/codex>
+   - Antigravity: Google's official Antigravity download page. ATLAS never runs Antigravity; you use it yourself in Step 14.
+2. **Check** each is installed: `claude --version`, `codex --version`, `agy --version`.
+3. **Sign in to each one yourself**, in your terminal. ATLAS never signs in for you and never reads these logins.
+   ```bash
+   claude          # Claude Code: follow the sign-in prompt, then exit
+   codex login     # Codex: sign in with ChatGPT (or another method Codex supports)
+   agy             # Antigravity: follow its sign-in prompt, then exit

+
+**For setup B:**
+1. **Install** a local model server (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM or `llama-server`) from its official site, and the Codex CLI (link above), which ATLAS uses to drive a local model as a developer.
+2. **Download** at least two models from different families, e.g. a Qwen coder model and a Llama model. With Ollama, for example: `ollama pull <model>`.

+   ```

+✅ **Done when** each CLI starts without asking you to sign in (setup A), or your local model server lists your models (setup B).
+
+### Step 4. Create a GitHub token for each repository
+**Available:** [today]
+ATLAS uses one **fine-grained PAT per project**, limited to that single repository (D3). It will not use your normal `gh` login.
+
+1. On GitHub, open **Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token**.
+2. **Repository access:** choose *Only select repositories* and pick **one** repository.
+3. **Repository permissions:** set exactly these:
+
+   | Permission | Access |
+   |---|---|
+   | Contents | Read and write |
+   | Pull requests | Read and write |
+   | Actions | Read |
+   | Checks | Read |
+   | Commit statuses | Read |
+   | Metadata | Read |
+   | Administration | Read (lets ATLAS read branch protection) |
+
+   **Do not grant** Workflows (write), Administration (write) or Secrets.
+4. Click **Generate token**. Keep the page open, or copy the token somewhere temporary and safe: you store it in Step 9, once ATLAS has given the project its id.
+
+ATLAS checks the token's permissions automatically when you register the project (Step 9). A stand-alone check script (`verify-github-pat.sh`, which never prints the token) is part of decision D3 but isn't published in this repository yet.

-## 1.5 What projects can be tested in this release **[P4]**
-Check these before registering a project:
-- **Linux toolchains only.** Projects that need macOS toolchains (Xcode, Swift for iOS/macOS, macOS-only binaries) can't be tested; testing is blocked.
-- **Tests must not write to tracked files.** Tests may write only to declared `writable_paths` and `/tmp`.
-- **No network during tests.** Dependency *installation* may use approved registries through ATLAS's allowlist proxy. Tests themselves always run with no network, so integration tests that call external services aren't supported yet.
-- **No Git submodules, no Git LFS**, and no symlinks that point outside the repo.
-- **No repository Dockerfile builds.** Use an approved, digest-pinned public image.
-- **No fallback to running tests directly on your machine.** If a project doesn't fit these rules, its testing is blocked (fail closed).

-## 2. Register a project **[P1 record; P5 protection discovery; P4 test config]**
-Dashboard → **Projects → Register repository**:
-1. Enter `owner/name`, e.g. `<your-github-user>/my-app`. ATLAS checks access, visibility and default branch.
-   - Public repositories: Codex is blocked (D5), and the default roles use Codex. A public project is therefore **blocked** until you make a new decision about a valid independent role assignment (ADR-005). You currently work only on private repos.

-2. **[P5]** ATLAS reads branch protection. If it can't, it asks you to declare the required CI checks and approvals; otherwise ATLAS will never merge on that project, and you merge on GitHub yourself (§4).

+- An unknown model family blocks until you set `model_family`.
+- If no agent can fill a role independently, the project shows `BLOCKED(agent_config)`.
+- Model servers must be on `127.0.0.1`. You can set `allow_remote_endpoint: true` for an agent, and the dashboard then warns you that your code leaves your machine.
+- Codex agents, with any billing, are blocked on **public** repositories (D5).
+- Results always show which model did the review. A small local model is allowed, but you can see what you're relying on.
+
+**Only if you chose `billing: api_key`:**
+- Store the key with **[P10]** `atlas secrets set <agent_id>`. Until then, use the commands in Step 9 with the service name `atlas.agent.<agent_id>`.

+- A CLI agent gets it only once ATLAS has proven that the CLI doesn't pass it on to the commands it runs. Until then that agent shows `BLOCKED(api_key_not_isolated)`. For `claude_cli` and `codex_cli`, this is proven or refuted in Phase 2.

+### Step 7. Set up the test sandbox (one time)
+**Available:** [P4]
+Tests run only inside Docker containers, in a dedicated Colima virtual machine (D11). This is the same on macOS and Linux. The exact flags are confirmed in Phase 4.
+
+1. **Reserve disk space** for the virtual machine. You need admin rights.
+   - **macOS:** create a dedicated APFS volume. First find your container ID:
+     ```bash
+     diskutil apfs list
+     ```
+     Then create an 80 GB volume, replacing `<container>` with that ID:
+     ```bash
+     sudo diskutil apfs addVolume <container> APFS AtlasSandbox -reserve 80g -quota 80g
+     ```
+   - **Linux:** create a dedicated partition, or a fixed-size LVM logical volume (e.g. 80 GB), and mount it where ATLAS's Settings page says.
+2. **Start the ATLAS virtual machine.** Open **Dashboard → Settings → Test sandbox** and run the exact command shown there. It stores the VM's data on the volume from step 1 and shares **no** folders from your computer. ATLAS refuses to run tests if the VM can see any of your folders.
+3. **Run the self-test** from the same page.
+
+✅ **Done when** Settings → Test sandbox shows the sandbox as ready. If it isn't ready, projects show `BLOCKED(no_test_sandbox)` with the reason, and no tests run: ATLAS never runs tests or dependency setup outside the sandbox. (Developer agents are different: they edit code in worktrees on your computer, inside their own CLI sandboxes. See [Part 8](#part-8-what-atlas-will-never-do).)

+## Part 3. Add a project
+
+### Step 8. Check that your project is supported
+**Available:** [P4]
+Before adding a repository, check that it fits these limits:
+- [ ] **Linux toolchains only.** Projects that need macOS toolchains (Xcode, Swift for iOS/macOS, macOS-only binaries) can't be tested.
+- [ ] **Tests don't write to tracked files.** Tests may write only to declared `writable_paths` and `/tmp`.
+- [ ] **Tests don't need the network.** Installing dependencies may use approved package registries, through ATLAS's allowlist proxy. Tests themselves always run without network, so integration tests that call external services aren't supported yet.
+- [ ] **No Git submodules, no Git LFS**, and no symlinks that point outside the repository.
+- [ ] **No Dockerfile from the repository.** Tests use an approved, digest-pinned public image.
+- [ ] **The repository is private.** Public repositories block Codex (D5), and the recommended setup uses Codex. A public project is therefore **blocked** until you make a new decision about an independent role assignment (ADR-005).
+
+If a project doesn't fit, its testing is blocked. ATLAS never falls back to running tests directly on your computer.
+
+### Step 9. Register the repository and store its token
+**Available:** [P1 registration and token check, P5 token use and protection discovery]
+1. Open **Dashboard → Projects → Register repository**.
+2. Enter the repository as `owner/name`, e.g. `<your-github-user>/my-app`. A repository can be registered only once.
+3. ATLAS shows the new project's **id**. Store the token from Step 4 under that id. The command asks for the token without showing it, so it doesn't end up in your shell history:
+   ```bash
+   # macOS (Keychain)
+   security add-generic-password -s "atlas.<project_id>.github" -a "<your-github-user>" -w
+
+   # Linux (Secret Service)
+   secret-tool store --label="ATLAS GitHub <project_id>" service "atlas.<project_id>.github" username "<your-github-user>"
+   ```
+   **[P10]** `atlas secrets set github <project_id>` does the same on either OS.
+4. ATLAS checks the token's permissions, your access, the repository's visibility and its default branch. A missing or weak token shows `BLOCKED(github_credential)`. ATLAS never falls back to your `gh` login.
+5. **[P5]** ATLAS reads the branch protection rules. If it can't, it asks you to declare the required CI checks and approvals. If you don't, ATLAS never merges on that project, and you merge on GitHub yourself ([Step 13](#step-13-follow-each-phase-and-approve-the-merge-d6)).
+
+### Step 10. Review and approve the project settings
+**Available:** [P1; tests P4]
+ATLAS proposes the project's settings from what it detects. You review them and approve. Anything the repository itself suggests is treated as untrusted until you accept it. The settings are saved at `~/.atlas/projects/<id>/project.yaml`:

    23	## Part 0. ATLAS in one minute
    24	
    25	ATLAS is a program you run on your own computer. You give it a software task for one of your GitHub repositories, for example "Add Google OAuth login". ATLAS then:
    26	
    27	1. asks one AI agent to **plan** the work as small phases;
    28	2. asks a **different** AI agent to **challenge** the plan;
    29	3. waits for **you** to approve the plan;
    30	4. for each phase: an agent **writes the code**, ATLAS **runs the tests** in a locked-down container, another agent **reviews** the code, and a QA step **checks** it;
    31	5. opens a pull request and waits for **you** to approve the merge.
    32	
    33	You stay in control: nothing is built before you approve the plan, and nothing is merged before you approve the merge.
    34	
    35	### Words used in this guide
    36	| Word | Meaning |
    37	|---|---|
    38	| **Agent** | An AI coding tool ATLAS can use, such as Claude Code, Codex, or a local model. You bring your own |
    39	| **Role** | A job in the workflow: *architect* (plans), *challenger* (attacks the plan), *developer* (writes code), *reviewer* (reviews code), *qa* (checks the result) |
    40	| **Model family** | Who made the model, e.g. Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT/Codex), Google (Gemini), Alibaba (Qwen), Meta (Llama). Reviews must come from a different family than the author |
    41	| **Phase** | One small, separately mergeable piece of a task |
    42	| **Candidate commit** | The exact commit that was tested and reviewed. Only this commit may be merged |
    43	| **Sandbox** | The Docker container, in its own virtual machine, where ATLAS runs tests. Tests never run directly on your computer |
    44	| **PAT** | A GitHub *Personal Access Token*: a password-like key that lets ATLAS work on one repository |
    45	| **Dashboard** | ATLAS's web page. It runs only on your computer, at `127.0.0.1` |
    46	| **BLOCKED / PAUSED** | ATLAS stopped and needs something from you. [Part 7](#part-7-troubleshooting-what-each-state-means) explains each one |
    47	
    48	LangGraph is ATLAS's **internal** workflow engine (ADR-001, ADR-006). You never use it directly; there's nothing to install, configure or pay for.

    51	
    52	## Part 1. Prepare your computer
    53	
    54	### Step 1. Check your operating system
    55	**Available:** [today]
    56	ATLAS runs on **macOS** or **Linux** (D13). Windows isn't supported yet; WSL2 may come later.
    57	
    58	Each person installs their own copy of ATLAS and uses their own accounts and models (ADR-007). There is no shared, hosted ATLAS.
    59	
    60	### Step 2. Install the required tools
    61	**Available:** [today]
    62	| Tool | Why ATLAS needs it | Check it's installed |
    63	|---|---|---|
    64	| `git` | Works with your repositories | `git --version` |
    65	| `gh` (GitHub CLI) | Opens pull requests and reads CI results | `gh --version` |
    66	| Python 3.12 | ATLAS is written in Python | `python3.12 --version` |
    67	| `uv` | Installs ATLAS's Python packages | `uv --version` |
    68	| Node 24 | Builds the dashboard | `node --version` (should print `v24…`; on macOS, follow Homebrew's printed note to add `node@24` to your `PATH`) |
    69	| Colima + Docker CLI | Runs the test sandbox (D11) | `colima version` and `docker --version` |
    70	| Linux only: QEMU + KVM | Lets Colima run its virtual machine on Linux | `ls /dev/kvm` |
    71	| A secret store | Holds your tokens safely | macOS: Keychain, built in. Linux: a Secret Service provider such as GNOME Keyring or KWallet, plus `secret-tool` |
    72	
    73	**On macOS**, with [Homebrew](https://brew.sh) installed:
    74	```bash
    75	brew install git gh python@3.12 uv node@24 colima docker
    76	```
    77	**On Linux**, install the same tools with your distribution's package manager (for example `apt` or `dnf`), or by following each tool's official install guide.
    78	
    79	✅ **Done when** every command in the "Check" column prints a version, with no "command not found".
    80	
    81	### Step 3. Set up at least two agents from different model families
    82	**Available:** [today]
    83	ATLAS needs **at least two agents from different model families**, because a change must be reviewed by a model from a different family than the one that wrote it (ADR-005). Choose one of these setups:
    84	
    85	| Setup | Agents you need | Notes |
    86	|---|---|---|
    87	| **A. Recommended** | Claude Code + Codex + Antigravity | Uses your existing subscriptions |
    88	| **B. Fully local** | Two or more open-weight models from different families, e.g. Qwen and Llama, served by Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM or `llama-server` | No subscriptions; code stays on your machine |
    89	
    90	**For setup A:**
    91	1. **Install** each tool by following its official install guide:
    92	   - Claude Code: <https://www.anthropic.com/claude-code>
    93	   - Codex CLI: <https://github.com/openai/codex>
    94	   - Antigravity: Google's official Antigravity download page. ATLAS never runs Antigravity; you use it yourself in Step 14.
    95	2. **Check** each is installed: `claude --version`, `codex --version`, `agy --version`.
    96	3. **Sign in to each one yourself**, in your terminal. ATLAS never signs in for you and never reads these logins.
    97	   ```bash
    98	   claude          # Claude Code: follow the sign-in prompt, then exit
    99	   codex login     # Codex: sign in with ChatGPT (or another method Codex supports)
   100	   agy             # Antigravity: follow its sign-in prompt, then exit
   101	   ```
   102	
   103	**For setup B:**
   104	1. **Install** a local model server (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM or `llama-server`) from its official site, and the Codex CLI (link above), which ATLAS uses to drive a local model as a developer.
   105	2. **Download** at least two models from different families, e.g. a Qwen coder model and a Llama model. With Ollama, for example: `ollama pull <model>`.
   106	3. **Start** the server so that it listens on `127.0.0.1` (your computer only), and check that it answers. With Ollama, for example:
   107	   ```bash
   108	   curl http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/models
   109	   ```
   110	
   111	✅ **Done when** each CLI starts without asking you to sign in (setup A), or your local model server lists your models (setup B).
   112	
   113	### Step 4. Create a GitHub token for each repository
   114	**Available:** [today]
   115	ATLAS uses one **fine-grained PAT per project**, limited to that single repository (D3). It will not use your normal `gh` login.
   116	
   117	1. On GitHub, open **Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token**.
   118	2. **Repository access:** choose *Only select repositories* and pick **one** repository.
   119	3. **Repository permissions:** set exactly these:
   120	
   121	   | Permission | Access |
   122	   |---|---|
   123	   | Contents | Read and write |
   124	   | Pull requests | Read and write |
   125	   | Actions | Read |
   126	   | Checks | Read |
   127	   | Commit statuses | Read |
   128	   | Metadata | Read |
   129	   | Administration | Read (lets ATLAS read branch protection) |
   130	
   131	   **Do not grant** Workflows (write), Administration (write) or Secrets.
   132	4. Click **Generate token**. Keep the page open, or copy the token somewhere temporary and safe: you store it in Step 9, once ATLAS has given the project its id.
   133	
   134	ATLAS checks the token's permissions automatically when you register the project (Step 9). A stand-alone check script (`verify-github-pat.sh`, which never prints the token) is part of decision D3 but isn't published in this repository yet.

   137	
   138	## Part 2. Install and configure ATLAS
   139	
   140	### Step 5. Install and start ATLAS
   141	**Available:** [P1]
   142	```bash
   143	git clone https://github.com/<owner>/atlas-orchestrator.git   # the URL of the ATLAS repository
   144	cd atlas-orchestrator
   145	uv sync                 # installs ATLAS (exact steps finalised in Phase 1 / Phase 10)
   146	atlas serve             # starts ATLAS and opens the dashboard in your browser
   147	```
   148	- The dashboard runs only on your computer (`127.0.0.1`) and is protected by a per-install session token.
   149	- ATLAS keeps its data in `~/.atlas/`: databases, logs and artefacts.
   150	- **[P10]** An install script, and an optional service that starts ATLAS when you log in: `launchd` on macOS, a `systemd --user` unit on Linux.
   151	
   152	✅ **Done when** the dashboard opens in your browser.
   153	
   154	### Step 6. Tell ATLAS about your agents
   155	**Available:** [P1 schema, P2 adapters, P10 CLI]
   156	Open **Dashboard → Settings → Agents** and add each agent from Step 3. **[P10]** `atlas agents add` does the same from the terminal. ATLAS saves the list in `~/.atlas/agents.yaml`. Edit agents only through the dashboard or the `atlas agents` command; a repository can never change this file.
   157	
   158	For each agent you choose an **adapter** (how ATLAS talks to it) and a **billing** mode.
   159	
   160	**Adapters:**
   161	| Adapter | Use it for | Roles it can fill |
   162	|---|---|---|
   163	| `claude_cli`, `codex_cli` (built-in, verified) | Claude Code; Codex with ChatGPT sign-in, an API key, or a local OSS provider | Any role |
   164	| `manual_handoff` (built-in) | A tool you run yourself, e.g. Antigravity | QA, or any read-only role |
   165	| `openai_compatible_http` | A local model server: Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, `llama-server` | **Read-only roles only** (challenger, reviewer) |
   166	
   167	Other agent CLIs aren't supported in this release. A new CLI is added only as a verified manifest in an ATLAS PR (ADR-007).
   168	
   169	**Billing** is set per agent and never changes on its own (D15):
   170	- `subscription`: uses the CLI's own login (Step 3).
   171	- `local`: uses your own model server.
   172	- `api_key`: uses an API key you store (see below). Only that agent ever receives it.
   173	
   174	If a subscription runs out, ATLAS **pauses**. It never moves the work to a paid API agent.
   175	
   176	**Example A, recommended (Claude + Codex + Antigravity).** This is what the dashboard saves:
   177	```yaml
   178	agents:
   179	  claude:      { adapter: claude_cli, models: [<claude model>], billing: subscription }
   180	  codex:       { adapter: codex_cli,  models: [<codex model>],  billing: subscription }
   181	  antigravity: { adapter: manual_handoff, provider: google, declared_family_required: true }
   182	```
   183	
   184	**Example B, fully local (no subscriptions):**
   185	```yaml
   186	agents:
   187	  local-coder:    { adapter: codex_cli, models: [qwen3-coder], model_family: alibaba,
   188	                    billing: local, endpoint: "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1" }
   189	  local-reviewer: { adapter: openai_compatible_http, models: [llama-4-maverick], model_family: meta,
   190	                    billing: local, endpoint: "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1" }
   191	  manual-qa:      { adapter: manual_handoff, provider: local, declared_family_required: true }
   192	```
   193	Model ids above are examples. Use the ones you actually run, pinned to exact versions (D10).
   194	
   195	**Rules ATLAS enforces for every setup:**
   196	- The reviewer, challenger and QA must come from a different provider **and** a different model family than the author (ADR-005). Two local models count as different providers, so for them only the family must differ.
   197	- An unknown model family blocks until you set `model_family`.
   198	- If no agent can fill a role independently, the project shows `BLOCKED(agent_config)`.
   199	- Model servers must be on `127.0.0.1`. You can set `allow_remote_endpoint: true` for an agent, and the dashboard then warns you that your code leaves your machine.
   200	- Codex agents, with any billing, are blocked on **public** repositories (D5).
   201	- Results always show which model did the review. A small local model is allowed, but you can see what you're relying on.
   202	
   203	**Only if you chose `billing: api_key`:**
   204	- Store the key with **[P10]** `atlas secrets set <agent_id>`. Until then, use the commands in Step 9 with the service name `atlas.agent.<agent_id>`.
   205	- HTTP agents get the key as a request header.
   206	- A CLI agent gets it only once ATLAS has proven that the CLI doesn't pass it on to the commands it runs. Until then that agent shows `BLOCKED(api_key_not_isolated)`. For `claude_cli` and `codex_cli`, this is proven or refuted in Phase 2.
   207	
   208	✅ **Done when** Settings → Agents lists your agents with no warnings.
   209	
   210	### Step 7. Set up the test sandbox (one time)
   211	**Available:** [P4]
   212	Tests run only inside Docker containers, in a dedicated Colima virtual machine (D11). This is the same on macOS and Linux. The exact flags are confirmed in Phase 4.
   213	
   214	1. **Reserve disk space** for the virtual machine. You need admin rights.
   215	   - **macOS:** create a dedicated APFS volume. First find your container ID:
   216	     ```bash
   217	     diskutil apfs list
   218	     ```
   219	     Then create an 80 GB volume, replacing `<container>` with that ID:
   220	     ```bash
   221	     sudo diskutil apfs addVolume <container> APFS AtlasSandbox -reserve 80g -quota 80g
   222	     ```
   223	   - **Linux:** create a dedicated partition, or a fixed-size LVM logical volume (e.g. 80 GB), and mount it where ATLAS's Settings page says.
   224	2. **Start the ATLAS virtual machine.** Open **Dashboard → Settings → Test sandbox** and run the exact command shown there. It stores the VM's data on the volume from step 1 and shares **no** folders from your computer. ATLAS refuses to run tests if the VM can see any of your folders.
   225	3. **Run the self-test** from the same page.
   226	
   227	✅ **Done when** Settings → Test sandbox shows the sandbox as ready. If it isn't ready, projects show `BLOCKED(no_test_sandbox)` with the reason, and no tests run: ATLAS never runs tests or dependency setup outside the sandbox. (Developer agents are different: they edit code in worktrees on your computer, inside their own CLI sandboxes. See [Part 8](#part-8-what-atlas-will-never-do).)
   228	
   229	---
   230	
   231	## Part 3. Add a project
   232	
   233	### Step 8. Check that your project is supported
   234	**Available:** [P4]
   235	Before adding a repository, check that it fits these limits:
   236	- [ ] **Linux toolchains only.** Projects that need macOS toolchains (Xcode, Swift for iOS/macOS, macOS-only binaries) can't be tested.
   237	- [ ] **Tests don't write to tracked files.** Tests may write only to declared `writable_paths` and `/tmp`.
   238	- [ ] **Tests don't need the network.** Installing dependencies may use approved package registries, through ATLAS's allowlist proxy. Tests themselves always run without network, so integration tests that call external services aren't supported yet.
   239	- [ ] **No Git submodules, no Git LFS**, and no symlinks that point outside the repository.
   240	- [ ] **No Dockerfile from the repository.** Tests use an approved, digest-pinned public image.
   241	- [ ] **The repository is private.** Public repositories block Codex (D5), and the recommended setup uses Codex. A public project is therefore **blocked** until you make a new decision about an independent role assignment (ADR-005).
   242	
   243	If a project doesn't fit, its testing is blocked. ATLAS never falls back to running tests directly on your computer.
   244	
   245	### Step 9. Register the repository and store its token
   246	**Available:** [P1 registration and token check, P5 token use and protection discovery]
   247	1. Open **Dashboard → Projects → Register repository**.
   248	2. Enter the repository as `owner/name`, e.g. `<your-github-user>/my-app`. A repository can be registered only once.
   249	3. ATLAS shows the new project's **id**. Store the token from Step 4 under that id. The command asks for the token without showing it, so it doesn't end up in your shell history:
   250	   ```bash
   251	   # macOS (Keychain)
   252	   security add-generic-password -s "atlas.<project_id>.github" -a "<your-github-user>" -w
   253	
   254	   # Linux (Secret Service)
   255	   secret-tool store --label="ATLAS GitHub <project_id>" service "atlas.<project_id>.github" username "<your-github-user>"
   256	   ```
   257	   **[P10]** `atlas secrets set github <project_id>` does the same on either OS.
   258	4. ATLAS checks the token's permissions, your access, the repository's visibility and its default branch. A missing or weak token shows `BLOCKED(github_credential)`. ATLAS never falls back to your `gh` login.
   259	5. **[P5]** ATLAS reads the branch protection rules. If it can't, it asks you to declare the required CI checks and approvals. If you don't, ATLAS never merges on that project, and you merge on GitHub yourself ([Step 13](#step-13-follow-each-phase-and-approve-the-merge-d6)).
   260	
   261	### Step 10. Review and approve the project settings
   262	**Available:** [P1; tests P4]
   263	ATLAS proposes the project's settings from what it detects. You review them and approve. Anything the repository itself suggests is treated as untrusted until you accept it. The settings are saved at `~/.atlas/projects/<id>/project.yaml`:
   264	
   265	```yaml
   266	# Only keys defined in the approved design are shown; unknown keys are rejected.
   267	project:
   268	  name: my-app
   269	  repository: <your-github-user>/my-app
   270	  base_branch: main
   271	agents:                      # agent ids from Step 6; the reviewer must differ from the author (ADR-005)
   272	  architect: claude
   273	  challenger: codex
   274	  developer: codex
   275	  reviewer: claude
   276	  qa: antigravity            # manual_handoff: you run Antigravity yourself (ADR-003)
   277	tests:                       # [P4]
   278	  writable_paths: [".venv", ".pytest_cache"]   # must not overlap tracked files (security-model.md §5.1.3)
   279	ci:
   280	  required_checks: []        # only needed if ATLAS can't read branch protection
   281	```
   282	For Example B, the roles would be: architect `local-coder`, challenger `local-reviewer`, developer `local-coder`, reviewer `local-reviewer`, qa `manual-qa` (you run QA with a non-Qwen model).
   283	
   284	**Test setup** isn't a fixed set of keys yet; the names are decided in Phase 4 and added here then. You will choose:

   450	- **Spend money you didn't choose to spend.** It uses API keys or paid API credits only for an agent you set to `billing: api_key`, and it never switches an agent's billing on its own.

Use the new packet | | Antigravity output isn't pure JSON | Ask it: "Output only the JSON object, no prose". Or extract the JSON block manually | | `agy` says authentication required | Run `agy` interactively once to sign in. ATLAS does not handle Antigravity sign-in | # ADR-007: Portable, self-hosted ATLAS with user-configured agents - Status: Proposed - Date: 2026-10-22 - Decisions: D13 (platforms), D14 (local and open-weight models), D15 (API-key billing) ## Context The Phase 0 design matched one machine: - agent roles were fixed to `claude | codex | antigravity` (agent-compatibility.md §5); - the platform was macOS only: Keychain, Colima on an APFS volume, Seatbelt and `launchd`; - examples used the author's GitHub account. Other people should be able to run ATLAS with the agents and models *they* have. That includes open-weight models served on their own machine. ## Decision ### 1. Distribution model - ATLAS is **self-hosted and single-operator**. Each person installs their own copy and runs it on their own machine with their own accounts. - A hosted or multi-user ATLAS that runs work through one person's subscriptions is still a **non-goal**. The provider terms cited in ADR-004 forbid it. - No account names, repository names or paths are hard-coded. Docs use placeholders such as `/`. ### 2. Agent registry Agents are configured by the user, not hard-coded. `~/.atlas/agents.yaml` is global, non-secret, schema-validated and rejects unknown keys: ```yaml agents: claude: # registry id, referenced by project roles adapter: claude_cli # a vetted adapter manifest (§3); provider derived: anthropic models: [claude-opus-5-5] # pinned explicitly (D10); no fallback models billing: subscription # subscription | api_key | local (D15) codex: adapter: codex_cli models: [] billing: subscription antigravity: adapter: manual_handoff provider: google # canonical provider, or local; required for manual_handoff (rule 4 below) declared_family_required: true # the user's imported result must name its model local-coder: adapter: codex_cli # same vetted adapter, pointed at a local OSS provider models: [qwen3-coder] model_family: alibaba # required for any model not in the built-in family map billing: local endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 local-reviewer: adapter: openai_compatible_http # read-only roles only (§4) models: [llama-4-maverick] model_family: meta billing: local endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 ``` Project roles refer to registry ids: ```yaml agents: { architect: claude, challenger: codex, developer: codex, reviewer: claude, qa: antigravity } ``` - **The roles above are a recommended profile, not built-in rules.** The policy engine checks every assignment against the adapter's allowed roles and against ADR-005 independence. - A project whose roles can't be satisfied is shown as `BLOCKED(agent_config)`, with the reason. - Each agent has three separate identities, all snapshotted with every execution and review (database-design.md): `agent_id` (the registry name), `provider` (who runs inference) and `model_family` (the model's lineage, ADR-005). The provider is derived in this order, and the first rule that matches wins: 1. `billing: local` **and** an endpoint that passes the loopback check (§4) → `local`. `billing: local` with a non-loopback endpoint is a config error, rejected at validation. 2. A remote endpoint (`allow_remote_endpoint: true`) → the user must pick `provider` from ATLAS's fixed list of canonical providers (e.g. `anthropic`, `openai`, `google`, `mistral`, `deepseek`, `together`, `groq`, `openrouter`). The hostname is never used as the identity, because two hostnames can belong to one operator. A remote endpoint with no declared provider is `unknown`, which counts as equal to every provider, so independence fails closed. 3. A hosted CLI with subscription or api_key billing → the manifest's provider (`claude_cli` → `anthropic`, `codex_cli` → `openai`). 4. A `manual_handoff` agent → the `provider` the user configures: a canonical provider (Antigravity → `google`) or `local` for a model the user runs on their own machine. ATLAS can't verify a manual run, so this is a recorded user declaration, like the model family. - The imported result must declare `model` and `provider`. A provider that differs from the agent's configured one is rejected. - With no configured provider, it is `unknown`, which fails independence closed. - Results keep the `manual_imported` evidence label. - `agents.yaml` is edited only through the dashboard or `atlas agents …` (Phase 10). Like project config, a repository can never supply or change it. ### 3. Adapter manifests (declarative, vetted) Each adapter `kind` is ATLAS code: `cli`, `openai_compatible_http` or `manual_handoff`. A **manifest** fills in the per-tool details for a `cli` adapter: - the argv template for each role, with no shell, using the same placeholder substitution and allowlisted values as the existing templates; - the output format and the parser to use (`stream-json`, `jsonl-events`, a final JSON file); - regex fixtures that map exit codes and stderr to capacity states; - the auth probe, the version probe and the flags the capability probe must find; - the env variables the tool needs. They come from the allowlist plus its own credential (§5), never the user's whole environment; - the config-isolation flags, for example Codex `--ignore-user-config` and Claude `--setting-sources user`. Each must have a hostile-config fixture test (security-model.md §3.2). **Only verified manifests load in this release.** A manifest is `verified` when it ships in the ATLAS repo with recorded fixtures and passes the hostile-repo and hostile-config tests. ATLAS refuses to load a user-added manifest: being assigned a read-only role doesn't make an unfamiliar CLI read-only, because the CLI could still run repository hooks or write to the worktree. A local copy of ATLAS can add a manifest only through a reviewed change to ATLAS itself. User-added manifests would need an independently enforced read-only filesystem and execution boundary, which is deferred. Until then, a user who wants another model without a vetted CLI uses the `openai_compatible_http` reviewer (§4). - There is no "run this command" or free-form shell adapter. - Built-in manifests in the first release: `claude_cli`, `codex_cli`, `manual_handoff`. Candidates added through the normal phase process include OpenCode, Aider, Goose and Gemini CLI. Each needs its own terms check, like ADR-003 and ADR-004. - **D5 is unchanged.** Every agent using the `codex_cli` manifest stays blocked on public repositories, whatever its billing. Narrowing D5 to ChatGPT sign-in would be a new user decision. ### 4. Local and open-weight models (D14) - **Write roles (developer, fixer)** use an *agent CLI* that supports local models, for example Codex with a local or OSS provider, or OpenCode. ATLAS does **not** implement its own tool-calling agent loop. That would be a new agent with a large attack surface, outside ATLAS's job. - **Read-only roles (challenger, reviewer)** may use `openai_compatible_http`. ATLAS POSTs one chat-completion request: - the request has a structured-output schema; - the context is ATLAS-assembled: the candidate diff and the plan, fenced as `UNTRUSTED`; - there are no tools and no function calling; - the reply is validated against the findings schema, just like CLI output. The evidence label is `agent_reported`. - **Endpoints are loopback-only by default** (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`, or a Unix socket). Any other host needs `allow_remote_endpoint: true` on that agent. The dashboard then shows that source code leaves the machine. The HTTP client: - resolves the host once and **connects to that validated address**; TLS still verifies the configured hostname; - **ignores proxy environment variables** (`HTTP(S)_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY`); - **rejects redirects**; - re-validates the address on every request. - **Local CLI providers** (e.g. Codex `--oss`) resolve their own endpoint, so ATLAS can't pin it. Before each launch, ATLAS checks that the configured provider endpoint is loopback, and the manifest pins that endpoint on the command line. Proxy variables are not passed to the agent (they are not on the env allowlist). Residual risk: the CLI's own network behaviour is trusted as published, like any verified CLI. - Local models have no quota; their capacity states come from HTTP status and timeouts. - A local model may be much weaker than a frontier model. Gate results show the reviewer's model, so the user can judge. ### 5. Billing and credentials (D15) - `billing: subscription` keeps ADR-004 unchanged. The CLI owns its login, and ATLAS strips every provider API-key variable. - `billing: api_key` is an **explicit, per-agent opt-in**: - the user stores the key with `atlas secrets set `; - ATLAS puts it in the OS secret store (§6) under `atlas.agent.`. - **Where the key may go.** An env variable passed to a CLI is inherited by every command the CLI runs, including commands steered by repository content. So: - For `openai_compatible_http` agents, ATLAS sends the key as an HTTP header. No subprocess ever sees it. - For a `cli` agent, the key is allowed only if the manifest declares `credential_isolation: verified`. That means a fixture test proves the CLI removes the key from the environment of every tool or shell command it launches: an agent-launched `env` dump must not contain it. The manifest names the one variable that receives the key. - If the manifest doesn't declare this, every role of that agent is `BLOCKED(api_key_not_isolated)`. A credential broker or runner design that would lift this is deferred. - Proving this for `claude_cli` and `codex_cli` is a Phase 2 spike item. Until then, both use `subscription` or `local` billing only. - Every other agent and every test, git and gh process still has all key variables stripped. - **Exact-value redaction.** Every secret ATLAS loads (PAT, API key, bearer token) is registered with the redactor **before** any launch or request that uses it. The redactor removes the exact value, in addition to known patterns such as `sk-…`, from all stdout, stderr, events, error messages and artefacts. Tests cover tokens that match no known pattern. - `billing: local` passes no credential. An optional bearer token for a local server is handled like an HTTP API key (header only, redacted). - **There is never a silent switch between billing modes.** - A subscription agent that runs out of quota pauses, as before. - ATLAS never retries a subscription agent's work with an api_key agent. `allow_paid_api_fallback` stays locked to `false`. - Moving a role to another agent is a config change the user makes, recorded in `audit_log`. It is not a fallback. - This changes ADR-004: ATLAS now *stores* API keys the user gives it. It still never reads, copies or proxies the subscription credentials that the CLIs manage. ### 6. Platforms (D13): macOS and Linux Platform-specific code sits behind small interfaces chosen at startup: | Interface | macOS | Linux | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | `SecretStore` | Keychain | Secret Service (GNOME Keyring / KWallet) via `keyring` | No plaintext-file fallback. If there's no backend, credential-needing operations are `BLOCKED(no_secret_store)` | | `TestSandbox` | Colima VM (`vz` / QEMU) | Colima / Lima VM on QEMU + KVM | **Same VM boundary on both.** No host mounts, explicit socket, everything in security-model.md §5.1 applies unchanged. Running Docker natively on the Linux host is rejected, because then containers share the host kernel and daemon | | Reserved disk for the sandbox VM | Dedicated APFS volume, reserve = quota | Dedicated partition, or a fully allocated (thick) LVM logical volume. Thin, sparse or loop-file backing is rejected after inspecting the backing device (`lsblk`, `lvs -o lv_layout`) | Same "reserved, not observed" rule (security-model.md §5.1) | | `AgentBoundary` (outer wrapper for agent processes) | Seatbelt (`sandbox-exec`) | bubblewrap, with Landlock where the kernel supports it | Same deny list. Proving it on Linux is a Phase 2 spike item. If it fails, shell-capable roles are `BLOCKED(no_agent_boundary)`, as on macOS | | Service manager (Phase 10) | `launchd` user agent | `systemd --user` unit | Optional | | Notifications (Phase 9) | macOS notifications | freedesktop notifications | Optional | - **Windows** is not supported natively. WSL2 may come later; it would use the Linux path. - CI runs the platform-independent test suite on both `macos-latest` and `ubuntu-latest`. The tests specific to each platform's sandbox and secret store run on the matching runner. ## Consequences - The Phase 1 config schema includes the registry. The policy engine checks roles against registry entries, not provider names. - Phase 2 builds adapters from manifests and adds one `openai_compatible_http` reviewer as proof that local models work. It also runs the `credential_isolation` and Codex `--oss` spikes. The Linux `AgentBoundary` spike sits next to the Seatbelt spike. - Phase 4 adds the Linux disk-reservation check. The VM boundary and its checks stay the same. - Phase 10 adds `atlas agents add | test | list` and `atlas secrets set`, plus a Linux service unit. - A user with only local models can fill every role, provided the registry holds at least two model families, e.g. Qwen as developer and Llama as reviewer and QA. ADR-005 enforces this. - The QA role may be any agent whose manifest allows `qa`, or the generic `manual_handoff`. The minimum QA gate (roadmap Phase 4) works with any of them. Antigravity is one manual-handoff profile, and it stays in the recommended profile. D4 still applies: an assignment is never changed while a handoff is pending. - More combinations of providers, models and operating systems means more to test. Only `verified` manifests load.

# ADR-005: Review independence is enforced by provider *and* model family

- Status: Proposed
- Date: 2026-10-22

## Context
Antigravity can run Claude and GPT-OSS models (`evidence/agy-models.txt`). Claude Code and Codex may also expose models from several families over time. If the reviewer and the author share a model family, they tend to share the same blind spots.

## Decision
- Every artifact (plan, phase diff, fix) records `author_agent` and `author_model`, plus the snapshot of the derived provider, model family and registry revision taken at execution time (ADR-007). Gates for past artifacts use these immutable snapshots, never the current registry.
- A reviewer, challenger or QA agent is assigned only if `provider ≠ author provider` **and** `model_family(reviewer_model) ≠ model_family(author_model)`.
- Model family mapping (built-in, versioned with ATLAS):
  - `claude-*` → anthropic;
  - `gpt-*` (including open-weight `gpt-oss-*`), `o*` and Codex defaults → openai;
  - `gemini-*` and `gemma-*` → google;
  - `llama-*` → meta;
  - `qwen*` → alibaba;
  - `mistral-*`, `mixtral-*`, `codestral-*`, `devstral-*` → mistral;
  - `deepseek-*` → deepseek;
  - unknown → `unknown`, which counts as matching the author's family, so independence is not satisfied.
- **Declared family (ADR-007).** A registry entry may set `model_family` for a model the built-in map doesn't know, such as a fine-tune or a renamed local model. The user's declaration is recorded with each artifact. If it contradicts the built-in map, the built-in map wins. A fine-tune counts as the family of its base model.
- **Provider identity (ADR-007 §2).** The "provider ≠ author provider" check compares the *derived* inference provider, not the registry id. It is derived by ADR-007 §2's precedence: `local` (only for validated loopback endpoints), a canonical declared provider for remote endpoints, or the manifest's provider. Two registry aliases or two hostnames for the same provider never satisfy it, and `unknown` matches every provider.
- **Local exception, stated explicitly.** The provider rule exists so that a single vendor's systems and policies can't both write and judge a change. Models running locally on the operator's own server share no vendor. So when **both** agents have provider `local`, the provider check counts as satisfied, and independence rests on the model-family check alone. In every other case, both checks apply.
- If independence cannot be met, the step goes to `AWAITING_MANUAL` or `BLOCKED`. The author is never used as the sole reviewer.
- A fix to a finding is "verified" only by an independent reviewer's re-check on the new SHA, plus re-executed tests.

## Consequences
- With user-configured agents, any profile is accepted only if every review, challenge and QA assignment passes these rules. A profile with a single model family can't run mandatory reviews, so those steps go to `AWAITING_MANUAL`.
- With the default roles, the developer is Codex (openai), the code reviewer is Claude (anthropic), and QA is Antigravity on a Gemini model (google). That gives three distinct families.
- Losing one provider may block mandatory reviews. This is intentional, because the brief requires that independence never be sacrificed.
